assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are a measurement advance of the first order. The magic-wavelength idea together with strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks gave stability and accuracy that redefine what can be measured, from relativistic geodesy and gravitational redshift tests to searches for variation of constants and dark matter. This is the clearest instance of a new measurement technique opening new ways of observing nature.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made early demonstrations; Ye's JILA group drove the record stability and systematic-uncertainty reductions and the precision applications. Both are exact credited names and form a natural two-person prize. Other contributors (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the theory of magic wavelengths) are outside the supplied credit, so some allocation ambiguity remains. I cannot independently verify the full history of early lattice-clock priority.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Multiple independent laboratories worldwide reproduce 10^-18-class performance, and the SI second redefinition path is under discussion. Recognition is timely, with the optical frequency comb already honoured in 2005.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second before recognising optical clocks.
Priority and credit among several international clock groups beyond the two credited names.
Overlap with earlier recognition of frequency combs and ion-trap clocks may be read as incremental.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled coherent interfaces between light and matter (cavity QED single-atom photon exchange, atomic-ensemble quantum memories, electromagnetically induced transparency and DLCZ-type storage) underlie quantum repeaters and networks. This is close to my own field of quantum memories, so I know how hard high-efficiency, long-coherence storage is; the field has opened a real research direction and enabled many other experiments.
assessment.attribution: Kimble (quantum network vision, cavity QED and ensemble experiments), Rempe (single-atom single-photon network nodes) and Lukin (EIT storage, ensemble and solid-state interfaces) are leading contributors. The topic is a compound area with several physical platforms (atoms, rare-earth crystals, NV centres, cavities); the committee would struggle to define a single discovery, and credit for rare-earth-crystal memories and photon-echo protocols (CRIB, AFC) sits outside the supplied names. I declare a possible conflict of interest as a practitioner in the area.
assessment.maturity: Maturing but not finished. Memory efficiency, storage times and multi-node entanglement have been demonstrated on several platforms, but a deployed quantum network has not arrived. Recognition is plausible but possibly premature for a clean prize citation.
uncertainties: Definition of a single citable discovery within a broad platform-diverse field.
Disputed or distributed credit for memory protocols across several groups.
Practical scalability to networks remains an open question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry delivers inertial sensing, gravimetry, tests of the equivalence principle and measurements of the fine-structure constant at very high precision. The measurement methodology is fundamental, and it connects to quantum sensing uses (geophysics, navigation) that I regard as important beyond physics.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometer with gratings), Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometry theory and early work) and Kasevich (atomic-fountain interferometers with Chu and high-precision gravimetry and gradiometry) are all credited. Steven Chu's role is notable but he is not in the supplied credit and already holds a Nobel prize for laser cooling; Kasevich's key early work was with him. This creates a genuine allocation difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Mature for gravimetry and constants; commercial instruments exist. Large-scale fundamental-physics applications (gravitational-wave detection, dark matter) are still developing, so the field is still active.
uncertainties: Credit allocation involving Chu, Chu's prior Nobel prize and other groups such as those of Rasel or Kasevich's students.
Whether the headline impact is a single discovery or a family of techniques.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable coupling of microwave photons to superconducting qubits routine, and it is the basis of dispersive readout and most current superconducting quantum processors. The technique has clearly enabled a very large body of follow-on work.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and the Yale experiment with Wallraff, so the supplied three-name set leaves out Andreas Wallraff and others. Within the credited names, Schoelkopf (experiment) and Girvin and Blais (theory) are the natural core. Recognition of superconducting-circuit physics in 2025 may reduce the room for a close successor.
assessment.maturity: Mature and heavily confirmed across laboratories and industry. Timing depends on the committee's appetite for another superconducting-circuit prize so soon.
uncertainties: Omission of Wallraff from the supplied credit weakens a clean allocation.
Possible proximity to the recent macroscopic quantum tunnelling prize in superconducting circuits.
Girvin also appears in other candidate groupings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light turns a quantum-noise limit into a resource and is now used operationally to improve gravitational-wave detector sensitivity. It is a clean example of a quantum measurement technique with a demonstrated payoff in a major instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-state interferometry in 1981; Kimble and colleagues performed early squeezed-light generation and applications, while Schnabel and the GEO600 and LIGO groups developed practical implementation. Slusher's first squeezing experiment and the contributions of Mavalvala and others, as well as Walls and Yurke, are not all in the proposed names, so allocation is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed, with squeezing routinely used in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600. The recognition would be timely, partly in light of the 2017 prize for gravitational waves.
uncertainties: Many contributors in the early squeezing history; unclear which two or three would be fair.
Impact is mostly in one instrument class, though it is widespread within quantum optics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Ti:sapphire gain medium and Kerr-lens and SESAM mode-locking made femtosecond lasers a robust, widely available tool. They are the backbone of ultrafast spectroscopy, multiphoton microscopy, frequency combs and attosecond science, much of which has already been recognised downstream.
assessment.attribution: Moulton demonstrated Ti:sapphire; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking and Keller developed semiconductor saturable-absorber mode-locking. The three-way split appears reasonable, though Kerr-lens work is shared with Spence and others and CPA recognition in 2018 overlaps in application.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of demonstrated impact. The risk is that this could be viewed as a technology that has been honoured through its applications and through the 2018 laser prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2018 chirped-pulse amplification prize and the 2023 attosecond prize.
Credit for Kerr-lens mode-locking is split among several groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers realise quantum simulation and gate-based computing with direct single-site control and readout. This is a striking set of experimental demonstrations that enabled many other experiments, with active experimental frontiers.
assessment.attribution: Lukin's group, Browaeys and Saffman each made central contributions to Rydberg blockade, tweezer arrays and gates, but credit with Bloch, Endres, Ahn, Weiss and Browaeys's peers is widely distributed. The credited triple seems defensible but certainly not unique.
assessment.maturity: Still young; error rates, scale and algorithmic usefulness are evolving. Recognition is probably premature, though the experiments themselves are well reproduced.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the pace of progress and error-correction milestones.
Distributed credit across several international groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and control of single NV spins in diamond enabled nanoscale magnetic, electric and thermal sensing with room-temperature operation. This is a direct example of a new measurement technique, with growing applications in condensed-matter physics and biology.
assessment.attribution: Gruber and Wrachtrup (single NV optical detection, 1997) are the decisive early experimental step; the sensing protocols (Maze, Taylor, Balasubramanian and Lukin) and Walsworth's work are also central. Balasubramanian, Jelezko and Taylor are not in the supplied credit, so the split is imperfect.
assessment.maturity: Maturing; many groups reproduce the results and commercial products exist, but quantitative metrological advantage over alternatives is still being defined in several areas.
uncertainties: Several key contributors (for example Jelezko and Balasubramanian) are absent from the supplied credit.
Whether this is a recognised discovery or a platform whose main impact is still ahead.
